text: al treatments used in- termittently. UK guidelines7 recommend initial treatment with fluconazole 150 mg every 72 hours for 3 doses fol- lowed by maintenance treatment of 150 mg once weekly. Alternatively initial treatment may be with a topical azole product for 10 to 14 days, followed by maintenance with topical clotrimazole 500 mg once weekly, oral fluconazole 100 mg once weekly, or daily oral itraconazole or ketoco- nazole. Yogurt preparations containing Lactobacillus spp. have been used in the treatment and prevention of vaginal candidiasis in an attempt to restore the natural vaginal flora but evidence to support their use is limited. Infection involving the nails and surrounding tissue is dif- ficult to treat. Chronic paronychia (infection affecting the tissue around the nails) is often resistant to treatment but may respond to prolonged application of topical imida- zoles or nystatin. Onychomycosis (infection affecting the nail itself) usually only responds to systemic antifungals. Treatment with oral itraconazole appears to be the most appropriate, although oral terbinafine has also been used.1 Primary prophylaxis against mucocutaneous candidiasis is not recommended for patients with advanced HIV infec- tion since this may select for resistant Candida spp.9 Due to similar concerns, secondary prophylaxis in immuno- compromised patients with mucocutaneous candidiasis is largely restricted to those with frequent or severe recur- rences, or those at risk of developing invasive disease, in which case oral fluconazole or itraconazole may be con- sidered.1,9 Invasive and disseminated candidiasis require systemic antifungal treatment. Intravenous amphotericin B, with or without flucytosine, has traditionally been regarded as the standard initial treatment in most infections but flucytosine is now infrequently used because of concerns over its bone-marrow toxicity in AIDS patients. Fluconazole, caspofungin, and a combination of amphotericin B (for 5 to 6 days) and fluconazole have been shown to be effective and now offer alternatives for initial antifungal therapy. Fluconazole may be used as first-line for clinically stable patients with uncomplicated candidaemia who have not recently received treatment with an azole and is preferred for infections with C. lusitaniae. Amphotericin B is used for other non-albicans infections, although there is some evidence of resistance developing in C. krusei and C. gla- brata.
